title: The Consultants in the Indian Mills
text:
Economists had long noticed that management practices and productivity go together, but it was hard to prove that better management actually caused better results. In 2008 a team led by Nicholas Bloom ran a real experiment with large cotton fabric firms near Mumbai.

The research team, working with an international consulting firm, offered free consulting to a randomly chosen group of plants. The advice focused on basic practices: keeping factories clean and organized, recording and fixing quality defects, tracking inventory, maintaining machines regularly and holding production meetings. A control group received only a brief diagnosis.

At the start, the plants were strikingly disorganized, with piles of yarn and garbage on the floors and stock left unrecorded. In the treated plants, quality defects fell sharply, inventory dropped and productivity rose by about 17 percent in the first year. Within three years, the treated firms had also opened more plants. When asked why they had not adopted such practices before, owners often said they had not known about them or had not believed they would pay off.
lesson: Many organizations lose a great deal simply by neglecting basic good practices. Before searching for a big new strategy, check whether the fundamentals are in place.
people: Nicholas Bloom, Benn Eifert, Aprajit Mahajan, David McKenzie, John Roberts
source: Bloom, N., Eifert, B., Mahajan, A., McKenzie, D., and Roberts, J. (2013). Does management matter? Evidence from India. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(1), 1-51.
